strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: aggressive post-training quantization for DiT-based real-world image super-resolution, where deployment cost is a real bottleneck and existing PTQ methods are mostly designed for U-Nets, LLMs, or text-to-image DiTs.

The proposed components are technically plausible and well motivated. H-SVD directly targets the loss of local residual structure under low-rank/outlier decomposition, while VaSMP and VaTMP use simple variance-based distortion arguments to allocate precision spatially and temporally.
The evaluation covers several real-world SR benchmarks and compares against a broad set of PTQ, DiT-specific, diffusion, PEFT, and SR-oriented baselines under both W4A6 and W4A4 regimes.
Ablations are useful: the paper separates the effects of H-SVD, VaSMP, and VaTMP, studies the SVD-L rank budget, and provides qualitative examples that help explain the perceptual improvements.
The method appears lightweight relative to calibration-heavy or retraining-based alternatives, especially for W4A6 where the claimed weight mixed-precision allocation is data-free.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. H-SVD is an intuitive extension of existing SVD/outlier-absorption quantization, and variance-based mixed precision follows standard rate-distortion reasoning. The contribution is useful, but it is more an effective engineering synthesis for a specific backbone/task than a fundamentally new quantization principle.

Some claims are overstated relative to the tables. The manuscript says Q-DiT4SR achieves SOTA performance broadly, but in W4A4 several baselines outperform it on MANIQA, and in W4A6 it is not uniformly best on every metric. The results are strong overall, but the wording should distinguish best average/overall behavior from per-metric dominance.

The empirical scope is narrower than the framing suggests. All experiments use DiT4SR as the only backbone, so it is unclear whether the method generalizes to other DiT-based SR architectures such as DreamClear or newer DiT variants.

The paper reports parameter and operation reductions but does not provide actual wall-clock latency, memory bandwidth, GPU throughput, or deployment measurements. For a deployment-motivated quantization paper, real hardware measurements would substantially strengthen the significance claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The code URL is left blank, and important implementation details are missing or underspecified, including exact selected SVD-L block sizes, layer-wise bit allocations, VaTMP segmentation constraints, seeds, quantizer calibration details, and how all baselines were adapted to the same DiT4SR setting.

The calibration-free language is somewhat confusing: VaSMP is data-free, but VaTMP uses a 32-image calibration set. The manuscript should be more precise about which components require calibration and what the total preprocessing cost is, including SVD computation.

The evaluation relies heavily on no-reference perceptual metrics, and the authors themselves note that MANIQA can behave counterintuitively under severe quantization. More human studies, distortion metrics, or task-specific perceptual validation would make the quality claims more convincing.

Limitations and broader impacts are thin. The paper lacks a substantive discussion of failure modes, dataset bias in real-world SR, hallucinated detail risks, privacy-sensitive restoration settings, or misuse in forensic/medical/surveillance imagery.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: aggressive PTQ for DiT-based real-world image super-resolution, where model size and compute are serious deployment barriers.

The proposed components are reasonably concrete: H-SVD separates global low-rank and local block-wise residual structure, while VaSMP/VaTMP give explicit variance-based rules for weight and activation mixed precision. The formulation is understandable and mostly coherent.

The experimental section compares against a broad set of recent quantization and efficient diffusion baselines across four real-world SR datasets and two low-bit regimes, and includes ablations for H-SVD, VaSMP, and VaTMP.

The results show useful empirical gains over many baselines, especially on MUSIQ, CLIPIQA, and LIQE, and the paper acknowledges that no-reference IQA metrics can behave inconsistently under heavily quantized diffusion models.
weaknesses: The central deployment claim is not sufficiently supported. The paper reports parameter and operation reductions, but does not provide wall-clock latency, memory bandwidth, kernel support, energy, or actual hardware speedups. Since H-SVD adds full-precision low-rank/local branches and some baselines have fewer reported parameters/ops, the practical efficiency advantage is unclear.

The fairness of the comparisons is under-specified. Several baselines are adapted from text-to-image, LLM, one-step SR, or PEFT settings, but the paper gives little detail on how they were tuned, calibrated, or budget-matched for DiT4SR. This makes the claimed SOTA status hard to verify.

The empirical claims are overstated. Q-DiT4SR is not uniformly best across metrics; for example, in W4A4, MANIQA often favors other methods. The paper itself notes metric unreliability, yet still relies heavily on these metrics to claim best overall performance.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript says code and models will be available but provides no actual link, and many implementation details are missing: exact quantization granularity, block-size search outcomes, DP constraints for VaTMP, calibration/inference protocol details, baseline hyperparameters, and whether reported operations count FP SVD branches realistically.

The novelty is incremental. H-SVD, Hadamard rotations, SVD residual handling, variance-based bit allocation, and temporal activation scheduling are all close to existing quantization ideas; the paper combines them for DiT-based SR, but does not provide enough analysis to establish a strong new technical insight.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. All experiments use a single backbone, apparently one scale factor, one GPU setting, and mostly perceptual/no-reference metrics. There is no user study, robustness analysis, downstream error analysis, or evaluation across different DiT SR architectures.

The limitations and ethics discussion is essentially absent. For real-world SR applications such as medical imaging, satellite imagery, and consumer photography, hallucinated details and misleading reconstructions are important risks, but the paper does not seriously discuss uncertainty, misuse, or failure modes.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practical problem: aggressive PTQ for Diffusion Transformer based real-world super-resolution, where existing diffusion or DiT quantizers are not obviously suited to texture-sensitive restoration.

The technical approach is coherent. H-SVD is a reasonable extension of low-rank residual handling, and the variance-aware spatial and temporal mixed-precision schemes are well motivated by simple rate-distortion arguments and by observed layer/timestep variance patterns.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the paper length, covering four real-world SR benchmarks, W4A6 and W4A4 regimes, many recent baselines, qualitative comparisons, and component ablations. The reported gains are especially convincing in the difficult W4A4 setting, where prior methods often collapse or degrade substantially.

The method appears practically attractive: it uses little calibration, targets a strong DiT4SR backbone, reports parameter/operation reductions, and includes implementation details such as the calibration set size, quantized blocks, softmax precision, scale factor, and hardware used.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with the main design choices tied to the observed failure modes of generic DiT quantization for super-resolution.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. The abstract says code and models will be available, but no actual URL is provided, and several implementation details needed to reproduce the exact schedules are underspecified, such as the DP segmentation constraint, bit candidate sets used in all experiments, block-size selection details, and baseline adaptation details.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic perceptual/no-reference metrics, while the paper itself notes that these metrics can be misleading for heavily quantized diffusion SR. A human preference study or stronger perceptual validation would make the central visual-quality claim more convincing.

The ablations are relatively narrow: most component analysis is on RealSR only, while the main claims concern robustness across multiple datasets and bit settings. It is therefore harder to tell whether VaSMP/VaTMP consistently explain the full gains across all benchmarks.

The speedup evidence is mostly theoretical through parameters/operations. Given the added H-SVD branches, Hadamard transforms, and mixed-precision scheduling, actual latency, memory bandwidth, and deployment measurements on target hardware would be important for an efficiency paper.

The scope is limited to one DiT-based SR backbone, DiT4SR. This is understandable for a focused paper, but it leaves open how well the method transfers to other DiT SR architectures or to different diffusion step counts/schedulers.

The manuscript does not include a visible limitations or ethics discussion. For real-world image restoration, it would be useful to discuss hallucinated details, possible misuse in forensic/medical/surveillance contexts, and when quantized SR outputs should not be treated as faithful reconstructions.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: aggressive PTQ for DiT-based real-world image super-resolution, where deployment costs are a real bottleneck.

The proposed components are well motivated: H-SVD targets local residual structure that global low-rank branches miss, while VaSMP/VaTMP use variance-based distortion arguments to allocate precision across layers and timesteps.

The empirical section is broad for a specialized compression paper, covering W4A6 and W4A4 settings, four real-world SR benchmarks, multiple recent baselines, ablations, runtime/memory profiling, calibration robustness, and a second DiT-SR backbone.
The results suggest meaningful practical gains: Q-DiT4SR remains close to the FP model under W4A6 and gives competitive W4A4 quality with around 4.5x end-to-end speedup and much lower peak memory.
The paper acknowledges metric mismatch and W4A4 artifacts rather than hiding them, and includes local artifact analysis to partially substantiate the detail-preservation claim.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is somewhat overstated. In Table 1, Q-DiT4SR is not consistently best across metrics; for example, SVDQuant has much better W4A4 LPIPS on DrealSR/RealSR, and several noisy methods score higher on MANIQA. The paper notes metric mismatch, but then still relies heavily on those same no-reference metrics for its conclusions.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Several baselines are generic diffusion or transformer quantizers and may require careful adaptation to DiT4SR; the manuscript gives limited detail on whether each method was tuned fairly under matched calibration, kernel, rank, and bit-budget conditions.

The parameter-budget story around H-SVD is confusing. The text repeatedly says the local branch is under a matched parameter budget, but the final model appears to include both global and local branches, increasing parameters and memory relative to simpler low-rank baselines. This weakens claims that improvements come at the same budget.

The theoretical justification for VaSMP/VaTMP rests on Gaussian/high-rate uniform quantization assumptions and variance as the main sensitivity proxy. This is plausible, but the paper does not validate these assumptions deeply or compare against stronger sensitivity criteria such as Hessian/activation reconstruction under similar cost.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code and models will be available but the URL is blank, and key implementation details such as exact quantized kernels, bit sets, DP segmentation constraints, calibration preprocessing, and baseline hyperparameters are under-specified.

The qualitative evidence is helpful but limited by small selected crops; there is no user study or systematic perceptual evaluation to resolve the known unreliability of no-reference IQA metrics for quantized generative SR.

The impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss risks specific to super-resolution, such as hallucinated details in medical/satellite/forensic imagery, despite those applications being named in the introduction.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant deployment problem: low-bit post-training quantization for DiT-based real-world super-resolution, where memory and inference cost are genuine barriers.

The proposed framework has a coherent structure: H-SVD for weight reconstruction, VaSMP for layer-wise weight bit allocation, and VaTMP for timestep-wise activation precision scheduling. The ablations suggest each component can improve at least some reported metrics.
The manuscript includes practical memory and runtime measurements rather than only theoretical compression ratios, and it acknowledges remaining W4A4 artifacts and kernel-support limitations.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not convincingly support the strong SOTA and quality claims. The evaluation relies heavily on no-reference IQA metrics that the authors themselves show can reward visibly noisy reconstructions; in W4A4, several baselines outperform Q-DiT4SR on MANIQA, SVDQuant is often better on LPIPS, and the FP model is frequently better than the quantized method. No human study or task-grounded validation is provided to resolve these metric contradictions.

The comparison to prior methods is hard to trust. Many baselines are generic diffusion or LLM/DiT quantization methods, and the paper does not clearly explain whether they were carefully adapted, tuned, or given comparable calibration and implementation effort for DiT4SR. Since quantization performance is very implementation-sensitive, this weakens the claimed superiority.

The technical novelty is incremental. H-SVD is a relatively direct extension of low-rank residual handling with block-wise rank-1 approximation, and VaSMP/VaTMP are variance-based mixed-precision heuristics derived from standard high-rate quantization assumptions. The paper does not provide enough theory or empirical stress tests to show these choices are robust beyond the selected setting.

Important methodological details are under-specified for reproducibility: the code link is absent, DP segmentation constraints for VaTMP are vague, exact bit budgets and mappings to hardware kernels are not fully specified, and the custom Triton implementation for SVD-L is only described at a high level.

The soundness of the efficiency claims is not fully established. The paper reports operation reductions and speedups, but also notes that arbitrary precision kernels are not actually used and that schedules are mapped to standard low-bit linear computations. Hardware changes across experiments are confusing as the settings mention RTX A6000 while runtime profiling uses RTX 4090 48GB.

Generalization evidence is thin. The main results are centered on one backbone, and the DreamClear experiment is limited and produces suspicious cases where W4A6 outperforms FP on several no-reference metrics, reinforcing concerns that the metrics are not measuring faithful restoration quality.

The ethics/impact discussion is perfunctory, especially given applications mentioned in medical imaging and satellite reconnaissance. Potential risks from hallucinated or artifact-amplified super-resolution in sensitive domains are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely deployment problem: aggressive PTQ for DiT-based real-world image super-resolution, where prior SR quantization work is less directly applicable. The contribution is useful and reasonably original in combining hierarchical global/local SVD with layer-wise weight and timestep-wise activation precision allocation.

The technical ideas are clearly motivated. H-SVD addresses the loss of local residual detail under low-rank decomposition, VaSMP gives a simple data-free variance-based allocation rule, and VaTMP formulates timestep activation precision scheduling as a distortion-minimization problem with dynamic programming.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the main task: results are reported on four real-world SR benchmarks under W4A6 and W4A4, with comparisons to many PTQ, DiT-specific, diffusion, and SR-oriented baselines. The paper also includes ablations for SVD-L rank, VaSMP, VaTMP, runtime/memory, generalization to DreamClear, calibration-domain robustness, and local artifact analysis.

The paper is unusually candid about evaluation quirks: it notes that noisy outputs can score well on some no-reference IQA metrics, and it explicitly discusses remaining W4A4 artifacts and the dependence of practical speedups on kernel support.

The measured deployment results strengthen the practical case: the reported W4A4 model reduces peak memory substantially and achieves about 4.5x end-to-end speedup, with a runtime breakdown that distinguishes theoretical operation reduction from realized speedup.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is somewhat stronger than the evidence supports. Q-DiT4SR is clearly competitive and often best on no-reference metrics, but it is not uniformly best across metrics: for example, SVDQuant has better LPIPS in several W4A4 settings, and some degraded methods score higher on MANIQA. The authors acknowledge metric mismatch, but this weakens conclusions based mainly on IQA scores.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. The abstract says code and models will be available, but no actual URL is provided. Several implementation choices that likely affect results are underspecified, including exact feasible block-size selection for SVD-L, DP segmentation constraints for VaTMP, calibration/inference costs, and details of the Triton/local-rank implementation.

The evaluation would be more convincing with stronger perceptual validation. Since the paper itself shows no-reference metrics can be misleading for quantized generative SR, the absence of user studies, expert pairwise preference, or more systematic artifact-oriented evaluation limits confidence in the claimed visual superiority.

The comparison to baselines may not be fully fair or transparent. It is unclear how much effort was spent adapting each baseline to the DiT4SR backbone, whether hyperparameters were equally tuned, and whether all methods used comparable calibration budgets and optimized kernels.

The method is specialized to DiT-style SR models with linear-layer-heavy backbones and Hadamard/SVD-friendly structure. Generalization is tested on DreamClear, which is helpful, but still narrow; broader architectural or task transfer is not established.

The ethics/impact statement is boilerplate despite mentioning applications such as medical imaging and satellite reconnaissance. The paper should discuss risks of hallucinated high-frequency details in safety-sensitive restoration and possible misuse or overtrust of super-resolved imagery.
